articles.title: Five signs an MVP has competing sources of truth
articles.meta_description: How to recognize when your MVP's frontend, backend, and data layers disagree — before scaling turns inconsistency into a business risk.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi
articles.problem: Early MVPs often ship fast by letting each layer own its own version of state. That works until users, investors, or regulators start asking which number is correct.

sections.heading: Balances differ by surface
sections.body: The dashboard shows a balance the wallet API does not recognize, or the admin panel reports holdings the customer app never displays. When two screens answer the same question with different numbers, you have at least two sources of truth — not a display bug.

sections.heading: Event logs and application state diverge
sections.body: Your ledger or event stream says a transfer completed, but the product database still shows pending. Teams patch around this with retries and manual fixes instead of reconciling the model. That is a sign the write path was never unified.

sections.heading: On-chain reads disagree with backend APIs
sections.body: A wallet shows an active position while your indexer returns empty, or a contract state differs from what your API caches. In fintech and digital-asset products, this gap often means you are serving two authorities without a reconciliation layer.

sections.heading: Feature flags hide inconsistent behavior
sections.body: Different cohorts see different outcomes for the same action because each feature branch introduced its own persistence rules. Flags are useful for rollout — not for papering over incompatible data models.

sections.heading: Nobody can answer "what is the source of truth?"
sections.body: If engineering, product, and support each point to a different system when asked where the canonical record lives, you have an architecture problem — not a documentation gap. Fixing it gets harder after product-market fit.

articles.title: What investors should examine before funding fintech architecture
articles.meta_description: Six diligence questions that surface rebuild risk in fintech stacks — ledger design, custody boundaries, authorization depth, and vendor dependencies.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi
articles.problem: Fintech pitches emphasize growth, margins, and regulatory posture. Investors should still ask whether the architecture can survive scale, audit scrutiny, and a failed vendor.

sections.heading: Ledger design and reconciliation discipline
sections.body: Ask how money movement is recorded, not just how it is displayed. A credible stack has an append-only ledger or event log, idempotent posting, and daily reconciliation to bank and partner statements. If balances are mutable rows without an audit trail, diligence should treat that as structural risk.

sections.heading: Custody and funds-flow boundaries
sections.body: Understand where customer funds sit, which entity holds licenses, and what happens when a banking or custody partner changes terms. Diagrams that skip settlement timing or commingling rules are a signal that operations may be carrying the real architecture.

sections.heading: Identity, fraud, and authorization depth
sections.body: Authentication is table stakes. Investors should examine step-up controls, device binding, admin authorization, and how privileged actions are logged. Fintech incidents often start with weak internal tooling rather than consumer-facing login.

sections.heading: Data lineage for regulatory and investor reporting
sections.body: Request one example of how a regulatory or board number is produced end to end. If the path crosses ad hoc spreadsheets, unmanaged replicas, or unnamed analytics databases, reporting risk is higher than the deck suggests.

sections.heading: Vendor and blockchain dependency assumptions
sections.body: Many products combine custodians, card processors, chain indexers, and internal services. Diligence should identify single points of failure, contract exit cost, and what happens when an external read disagrees with the application database.

sections.heading: Security investments that lag product velocity
sections.body: Post-PMF security work is expensive because it interrupts live flows. Ask whether secrets management, environment separation, dependency patching, and incident response are funded in the current plan — not deferred to after the next release.
